en: Section Two: Collecting the Explanations by the Śramaṇa of Changshui to Refute Perversion and Gradually Clarify True Vision. This section has two parts: First, refuting King Bimbisāra’s view of annihilationism; Second, recounting what Ānanda destroyed in his vows to distinguish the true from the false.
Part One: Refuting King Bimbisāra’s view of annihilationism. Sub-part One: Recounting what Ānanda destroyed in his vows to distinguish the true from the false.

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, felt serene in body and mind; they reflected that since beginningless time they had lost their original mind, mistakenly identifying with the delusive affairs of discriminating reflections based on conditioned objects.
Today I have attained awakening, like a child who has lost its milk suddenly encountering its compassionate mother.
I have realized that the mind which pursues sensory objects is but a shadowy phenomenon, and I have further recognized that the vision confronting these objects is immovable.

Reflecting back on days past, I recognized the delusive and lost the true; my wandering was profound and my confusion difficult to dispel. Fortunately, I have encountered this auspicious assembly and met with such a favorable time. Now that the milk of the Dharma nourishes me, it is like a child meeting its mother—is this not a source of great joy?

With palms joined in reverence, he paid homage to the Buddha, wishing to hear the Tathāgata reveal the true and the false, the real and the unreal within body and mind, and the nature of the two luminosities: that which is subject to arising and ceasing in the present, and that which is neither arising nor ceasing.

The preceding passage rebuked [the notion] that "this is not your mind," which was intended merely to make one recognize the falsity of consciousness; it nevertheless pointed out that all phenomena are manifestations of the mind alone.
This further clarifies that the falsity of these manifestations is fundamentally devoid of self-nature, being originally the single Truth.
The One True Reality has never wavered; how could all phenomena ever arise or perish?

The Buddha’s intention was to lead them to see the truth within their very delusions; thus, he confirmed that the perception directed toward objects is fundamentally unmoving, while extensively rebuking those who mistake external things for their own nature and thereby lose the true mind.

Ānanda could not fathom the Buddha’s profound intent; he presumed that the two natures of reality and falsehood were entirely distinct, and that beyond the realm of birth and extinction there existed something unarisen and undying.

If this were so, then the teaching of "mind-only" would be a hollow fabrication and the discourse on "false dharmas" would be a mere waste of words. To pursue the words while losing sight of the intent results ultimately in delusion and perversion.
Although he harbored doubts, he did not yet dare to express them in words; thus it is said that he "joined his palms, paid homage to the Buddha, and wished to hear [the teaching]," and so forth.
Second, the King of Aṅga cites external authorities to request proof of non-arising, in four parts:
first, citing external authorities to describe his doubts.
At that time, King Prasenajit rose and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, before I had received the instructions of the Buddhas, I saw Kātyāyana and Vairāṭiputra, both of whom said:
'After this body dies, there is annihilation; this is called Nirvāṇa.'"
"Kātyāyana is his clan name; his personal name is Kālodāyin. This non-Buddhist adheres to the view that all phenomena both exist and do not exist.
Sañjayin is his name, and Vairaṭī is his mother's title; this non-Buddhist gives rise to the view of spontaneity."
Although external doctrines are numerous, they do not transcend the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Since both of these belong to the category of the view of annihilationism, it is said that they all claim total extinction.
These heterodox proponents of divergent views fail to understand how the seeds of karma arise in succession; they falsely claim that death itself is nirvana.
"Although I have encountered the Buddha, I still harbor doubts. How may I manifest and realize this ground where the mind is neither born nor extinguished?
All those among this great assembly who are still subject to outflows likewise desire to hear this."
Foxes are by nature full of doubt; whenever they encounter ice, they listen for the sound of water before they will cross.

Having previously heard that after death there is annihilation, and now hearing that there is neither extinction nor birth, they waver in indecision as to which is right and which is wrong; hence the term "fox-like doubt" (*śaṅkā*).

King Ajātaśatru deeply understood what Ānanda held in his heart: that he sought the unarisen and undying beyond the realm of arising and ceasing. Although his mind offered a secret entreaty, his mouth did not utter a word; thus, by citing the doctrines of external schools, he hoped the Buddha would provide an exposition. On the surface, this was to refute the nihilistic views of non-Buddhists and make them understand that death is followed by rebirth; in depth, it was to lead Ānanda to realize that true reality is not separate from the deluded consciousness of arising and ceasing. Therefore, it is said: "I testify that this mind is the ground of non-arising and non-ceasing."
2. An Account of the Body’s Transition and Transformation, in four parts:
1. A Question and Answer on Whether the Body is Permanent or Impermanent.
The Buddha addressed the Great King:
"While your body is present before me, I ask you this again: does this physical body of yours abide eternally and remain indestructible like a vajra, or will it eventually decay and perish?
"World-Honored One!"
"This present body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction.

When the Buddha raised this question, he intended to reveal that within birth and extinction there is non-birth and non-extinction, just as when one previously shook one's own head, one perceived nothing that moved.
2. Question and Answer on Knowing Extinction Without Having Yet Extinguished.
The Buddha said: "Great King!"
“You have not yet perished; how then do you know of perishing?
“World-Honored One!

Although this body of mine, subject to impermanence and decay, has not yet perished, I observe that it undergoes transformation and passes away from moment to moment, with nothing remaining constant as it is ever renewed. Like fire turning to ash, it gradually wastes away and dissolves; its destruction never ceases, and I am certain that this body must eventually reach total extinction.”
The preceding thought ceases and the succeeding thought arises; there is momentary transformation, like fire consuming wood which inevitably leads to total extinction.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) possess momentary cessation."
3. Question and Answer on the Appearance of the Old and the Young.
The Buddha said: "It is so."
"Great King!
Your present age has already reached old age; how does your appearance compare to that of your youth?
The King recounted that impermanence shifts and passes away from moment to moment, and that this principle is necessarily so; thus, he confirmed it as such.
He wished to further describe the phenomena of transition and decline, posing a question by comparing the old with the young.
At fifteen, one is called a "tóng" (child), as they have not yet received the capping ceremony.
"Líng" means age or years.

“World-Honored One! In my former childhood, my skin and flesh were moist and lustrous; as I reached adulthood, my blood and vital energy were full and robust. Now, in my declining years, I am pressed by senility; my appearance is withered and emaciated, my spirit is clouded and dim, my hair is white and my face is wrinkled. As my end approaches, how can I compare myself to those times of full vigor?”
One who has just been born is called a "hái" (infant); one who has just begun to walk is called a "rú" (child).
"Rú" means "moist"; it refers to being moist and weak.
"Fū" means "to spread"; it refers to being spread over the surface.
When the patterns and textures are radiant and beautiful, it is called *cou* (the skin).
These are all characteristics of childhood.
"Growing up" refers to the time of becoming an adult; this spans from the age of twenty onwards until the period of full vigor, which is why it is said that the blood and qi are fully replete.
My declining years are now sixty-two; my age is worn and decrepit, approaching seventy, which is why it is said that I am pressed by senility.
How can the World-Honored One see me as being comparable to them, given the difference between old and young?
4. Questions and Answers on Sudden and Gradual Approaches and the Passage of Time.
The Buddha said: "Great King!
"Your physical appearance should not have decayed so suddenly.
The preceding passage described the transformation of physical marks; the present question concerns the transformation of age. It is due to the transformation of age that one's marks undergo change.
The phrase "not decaying so suddenly" serves to describe how aging occurs gradually, with the moments of consciousness shifting from instant to instant.
The King said:
"World-Honored One!
The subtle shifting of transformations I truly do not perceive; yet the passage of cold and heat has gradually brought me to this state."

Why is this? Although I am twenty years old and thus called young, my countenance is already aged compared to when I was ten; at thirty, I was more decrepit than I was at twenty; now that I have passed sixty-two, looking back at the time I was fifty, I appear as distinctly robust as ever.
"World-Honored One!
I perceive their subtle shifting; although this [body] undergoes decay, the interval of its transformation is limited to ten years.
To set ten years as a limit is to observe according to coarse appearances.
*Cu* (passing away) means to go.
*Luo* (falling) means not remaining.
Since youth and vigor do not remain, one goes forth without returning; thus, "passing away and falling" refers to the process of flowing, changing, and transforming.
"If I were to reflect upon it more subtly, would its transformation be merely one or two *ji*? In truth, it is a change of years.
This takes a single year as the limit; changing and transforming year by year, how could it be anything less than ten years?
"Twelve years constitute a *ji* (a cycle).
It is not only that the years change, but it also involves the transformation of months.
This takes a single month as the limit; each month is different, not merely constrained by the year.
"How can it be that they change monthly, while moreover, they shift daily?
"How can it be" (*he zhi*) means "not only.
This takes a single month as its limit; yet [the changes] become more corrupted day by day, not merely on a monthly basis.
The above four limits of observation regarding the characteristics of impermanence, proceeding from the broad to the narrow, are still coarse and superficial; they do not yet constitute the subtle.

"Contemplating with deep reflection, one sees that between every moment and every thought there is no staying; thus one knows that this body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction."
This is an observation of the most subtle [level].

If one observes with a mind that is profoundly still and discerning, one sees that there is no cessation for even a single kṣaṇa; every thought-moment flows and transforms. This is precisely the incessant flux of the four subtle characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The minds of ordinary beings are coarse and thus remain entirely unaware.

As an ancient master said in verse: "If one were to place a single eyelash upon the palm of the hand, a person would not notice it; yet if placed upon the eye itself, it causes such distress and harm that there is no peace."

"The fool is like the palm of his hand; he does not perceive the transition of conditioned suffering. The wise man is like his own eyes; when confronted with the extreme, he gives rise to weary revulsion.
What is called a "kṣaṇa" (moment) is the smallest unit of time.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The shortest unit of time is called a *kṣaṇa*; the longest unit of time is called a *kalpa*. Even years and months are all divisions of time."

It is further stated: "One hundred and twenty kṣaṇas constitute one tatkṣaṇa; sixty tatkṣaṇas constitute one lava; thirty lavas constitute one muhūrta; thirty muhūrtas constitute one day and night; thirty days and nights constitute one month; twelve months constitute one year; and twelve years constitute one cycle."
The previous limit of ten years was merely a round number cited for the sake of a decade.
Third, demonstrating that the nature is not extinguished, in three parts:
first, the Buddha asks whether it is not extinguished, and the King replies that he does not know.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"You perceive that transformations and changes ceaselessly occur, and you thus realize your own extinction;
yet at the moment of this extinction, do you know that there is something within your body that does not perish?"
King Prasenajit joined his palms and said to the Buddha, “I truly did not know.
The coarse characteristics of arising and ceasing are as previously understood; the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing is also within your own body—do you recognize it?
King Bimbisāra raised an external doubt to prompt the World-Honored One for a clear exposition; now, having been questioned by the Buddha, he replied that he did not know.
Second, [the Buddha] granted the teaching on non-arising and extensively distinguished its unalterability.

From this point downward, the text clarifies the nature of seeing by observing that the river remains unchanged as the King grows from childhood to adulthood; the intent is to reveal that within the processes of arising and ceasing, one realizes the non-arising and non-ceasing, such that although the manifestations are coarse and proximate, their underlying meaning is profoundly subtle.

The first causes King Bimbisāra to verify coarse characteristics and awaken to the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings; the second causes Ānanda to give rise to profound understanding and know that cessation is fundamentally non-ceasing.
Thus, the manifestation of characteristics reveals the nature—this is the implicit discourse herein.
The head moves of its own accord, yet one perceives nothing moving; this is the meaning of this passage.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "As one contemplates the true reality of one's own body, so too does one contemplate the Buddha."
Master Sengzhao held that all phenomena are non-transmigratory (*apravartana*), not merely in terms of perception.
This meaning is clearly revealed at the beginning of the subsequent passage where the Buddha answers Mañjuśrī and unifies the three categories of existence.
Section Two:
First, granting the demonstration of non-arising.
The Buddha said:
"I shall now show you the nature that is neither born nor extinguished.
This permits the demonstration of the principle of non-arising at the very moment of arising and ceasing.
Second, the extensive investigation through interrogation, in three parts:
1. The Initial Question and Answer Regarding the River of Views: “Great King!
At what age did you first see the waters of the Ganges?”
The king said:
"When I was three years old, my compassionate mother took me to visit the god Jīvaka; as we passed by this stream, I immediately recognized it as the waters of the Ganges."

"Jīva" is translated here as "Life. It is the custom in the Western Regions to serve the deity of Longevity; when a child reaches three years of age, they visit that temple to offer thanks for having been granted life.
This inquiry regarding seeing through the medium of years intends to show that while the years change, what is seen remains unchanged.
Second, the question and answer concerning the similarities and differences regarding the river of views.
The Buddha said:

“Great King! As you have said, at twenty one declines from ten, and so on until sixty; as days, months, years, and seasons pass, they shift and change moment by moment. Thus, when you were three years old and saw this river, how was its water when you reached the age of thirteen?”
The King said: "It is exactly as it was when I was three years old; even now at sixty-two, there has been no difference.
These words regarding "no difference" are worthy of profound reflection; though they may seem superficial at first glance, upon further consideration, they contain deep significance.
3. Question and Answer on Perceiving Youth and Old Age.
The Buddha said:

"Now that you yourself perceive your hair to be white and your face wrinkled, your face must certainly be more wrinkled than it was in your youth. Thus, as you now look at this Ganges River, is there any difference between the perception of the river now and the perception of the river when you were a child—any sign of youth or old age?"
The king said, “No, World-Honored One.”

"The coarse characteristics of the physical body—whether it be childhood or old age—are easy to discern; however, the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*), which does not undergo transition, is truly difficult to awaken to.
By distinguishing between these two, one is led to realize non-arising (*anutpāda*)."
3. To clarify the constant nature and refute their doubts, the Buddha said:
"Great King!..."
Although your face is wrinkled, this essence of seeing has never been wrinkled.
That which wrinkles is subject to change; that which does not wrinkle is not subject to change.
That which changes undergoes extinction, but that which is unchanging fundamentally lacks birth and death. How, then, could birth and death affect it within this?
"Kè points to the constant nature (changxing).

Arising and ceasing merely involve the transformation of the conditioned; the unconditioned does not undergo birth and death. If one knows that which is immutable, one immediately perceives non-arising."
"And yet you still cite those such as Makkhali and others, saying that after the death of this body there is total annihilation?
This rebukes their skepticism. "Makkhali" is his personal name;
his mother's name was Kūsāli. This refers to one distinct from the person cited by King Nanda; both are non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika), and he is referring to them in that manner.
The transformation of the physical body may be described as impermanent, yet the nature of seeing does not shift; its principle is not subject to annihilation.
Fourth, faith and realization arise in succession.

Upon hearing these words, the King came to believe that after death one leaves this life to proceed to another birth. Together with the great assembly, he leaped for joy and rejoiced, attaining what he had never experienced before.
To describe their shallow understanding, it is said that they merely abandon one life to move toward another;
yet, when investigating their profound intent, one must know that the source of cessation is itself unceasing.
They have attained realization according to their capacity, with both the principal and the associates reaching the same goal, though this has not yet been explicitly stated.
2. Directly confronting Ānanda to refute his view of permanence, in two parts:
A. Ānanda raises a question based on a perceived contradiction.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, knelt down, and addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If this seeing and hearing do not arise or cease, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of perversion?”
"I pray that you will arouse compassion and wash away my defilements.

According to this, the view of the River of Views is no different from my own views and hearing; yet, regarding the King, it is said that he is neither extinguished nor born, while regarding me, it is said that I have lost the true nature.
Between the King and me, who is closer and who is more distant? If we follow divergent paths, how can they be distinguished?

However, the intent of this question has long been present; it originated from observing that though my hands open and close, there is no opening or closing, and though my head moves and shakes, there is no shaking or movement. Each of the Buddhas and Seals has declared it to be thus.
This means that the Tathāgata causes one to discern true vision within false vision itself, wherein there is no existence of non-arising-and-ceasing apart from arising-and-ceasing.

Ānanda, not yet understanding the Buddha’s intent, still maintained that arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-ceasing were distinct; he therefore joined his palms, prostrated to the Buddha, and requested to hear how the Tathāgata would manifest before them the true and the false, the real and the unreal of body and mind, and the two natures of illumination: arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-ceasing.

King Bimbisāra, knowing the king’s inner thoughts yet not wishing to question him further to clarify his sincerity, led forth the six heretical teachers who maintained that the self is annihilated after death. His hope was that the Buddha would personally provide an exposition so that he might abandon false views and realize the truth; thus, he urged Ānanda to refrain from making a distinction between the two.
How could the ancient Buddha Ānanda not have understood this?

It is because the delusions of those today are so heavy and their attachments so deep that they must be shown such bewilderment; thus, he spoke with firm insistence to reject their disputes, and for this reason he asked this question.
2. The Tathāgata’s Verification and Refutation of Clinging Sentiments, in three parts:
1. Verification that Reveals Inverted Sentiments, in two parts:
1. Using the Hanging Hand as a Question to Elicit the Sentiment of Permanence, in four parts:
1. Question. At that moment, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm, pointing downward with his wheel-marked hand, and said to Ānanda:
"Do you now see my *mudrā* hand as upright or inverted?"
"Pointing downward" refers to pointing down.
*Mudrā* is translated here as "seal.
This intention is to clarify that just as there are correct and inverted ways of seeing with the hand, so too there are correct and inverted ways of seeing [reality].
2. Answer. Ānanda said:
"The sentient beings of the world regard this as inverted, yet I do not know who is correct and who is inverted."
"This is how the people of the world regard it as inverted, yet I do not know what [the truth] is.
3. The Interrogation.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If worldly people consider this to be inverted, then what do worldly people take to be correct?
If they consider hanging the hands downward to be inverted, then what else would they take to be correct?"
4. Explanation. Ānanda said:
"If the Tathāgata raises his arm, with his hand as soft as tūla-cotton pointing upward toward the sky, this is called 'correct.'"
Raising one's hand is "upside down" (paryasta), while lowering it is considered "right side up"; because it does not accord with the body, this is deemed inverted.
Ānanda failed to distinguish between the real and the false, clinging to the false and losing the real; therefore, the Tathāgata rebuked him for acting in a perverted manner.

Since one has realized that the delusion is fundamentally without substance, one should understand that the truth is inherently quiescent; thus, it is granted that the seeing which moves toward an object and the nature that observes the river are themselves the true nature, with no separate truth existing apart from them.

Ananda, still not understanding as before, thought that the false was external while the true existed within; he consequently could not accept that he was a person of inverted views, nor that the King possessed the nature of non-arising.

After Ānanda had presented his questions regarding the dispute, the Tathāgata examined him based on these matters; yet, he could not distinguish between the conditions of the contrary and the compliant, and his state of inverted attachment was difficult to liberate.
The following text proceeds to refute this.
2. Raising the Arm to Demonstrate the Rectification of Inverted Views.
The Buddha then raised his arm and said to Ānanda:
"If this [arm] were inverted such that the head and tail were exchanged, people of the world would look at it with double the attention."
Since it was stated that holding up the arm constitutes the correct [position], the Buddha then held up his own arm and proceeded to reprimand him; this is precisely a case of inversion.
Originally the finger pointed downward, but now it has been turned upward; therefore, it is said that "the beginning and the end have been exchanged."

Worldly people do not rely on their fundamental nature to regard what is correct as correct; instead, they give rise to divergent views, regarding what is inverted as correct. Therefore, it is said that they "view with a single-sided gaze.

Thus you should know that when your body is compared to the pure *dharmakāya* of all Tathāgatas, the body of a Tathāgata is called "Right Universal Knowledge" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*), while your own bodies are termed "inverted by nature."

If one examines it by this standard, one will know that when your body and the Tathāgata’s body are compared, they are analogous; yet, while the Buddha-body is clearly revealed as upright, your body should be seen as inverted.
Furthermore, if one uses the hand seen by the Buddha as an analogy to reveal the Buddha’s body, it is clear that the Buddha’s body is named "Perfectly All-Knowing" (Samyak-saṃbuddha).
If one uses the hand seen by you to compare with your own body, it is clear that your body is designated as "Inverted in Nature."
Are you not acting in a state of perversion?

One who possesses "Right Universal Knowledge" (Samyaksaṃbuddha) is called "Right" because they are free from perversion, and "Universal Knowledge" because they have exhausted the entirety of the Dharma-realm.
Ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles do not bear this title because they are all subject to perversion.
2. To inquire about the locus of inversion, there are two parts:
first, inquiring about where the inversion resides.
"Examine your own body and the Buddha’s body with careful attention; if you designate them as 'inverted,' at what point in their names or characteristics do you label them as inverted?"
"Follow" means to comply with.
Comply with your own mind and examine it thoroughly: if the Buddha were inverted, where in the Buddha-body would you say the inversion lies?
If you are inverted, then at which part of your own body do you designate the name "inversion"?
This is intended to make him recognize the locus of his cognitive inversion (*viparyāsa*).

The character for "name" (*míng*) is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*), just as it is used to designate the eyes; ancient masters interpreted this as the dissolution of marks (*xiàng*), which consequently caused the subsequent scripture’s precise analysis of the lineage of inversion (*viparyāsa*) to lack coherence, resulting in it becoming a disconnected interpolation.
Since he has already severed both the correct and the inverted, why does the Tathāgata speak of inversion again?
Let students examine this carefully; do not seek glory by praising antiquity.
Second, an account of their ignorance.

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly gazed at the Buddha with fixed, unblinking eyes; they were so transfixed that they were unaware of the location of their own bodies and minds or their inverted perceptions.
"Deng" (瞪) means the manner of staring straight ahead.
"Blindly" (*mèng*) means being dazed and confused, lacking clarity.
Hearing that the point of overturning [delusion] was so obscure as to be unintelligible, he could not utter a single word; he simply knew to gaze directly at the Buddha.
3. Extensively demonstrating the characteristics of perversion, in two parts:
First, giving voice to compassion and addressing the assembly to recount what is commonly taught.
The Buddha, arising in great compassion and out of pity for Ānanda and the great multitude, uttered a voice like the ocean tide to address all those gathered together:
“O sons of good family!
I have always taught that all conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and their objects, are manifested solely by the mind.”
"The celestial drum has no thought, yet it resonates in accordance with people;
the ocean tide has no intention, yet it never misses its appointed time.
This symbolizes unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*), which speaks in response to the capacity of beings without waiting for a request."
"Matter" refers to the eleven kinds of matter;
"mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings;
"all conditions" generally indicates both matter and mind, or may specifically indicate the formations dissociated from mind.
The mental factors consist of the fifty-one mental concomitants.
All objects of cognition refer to the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

These five categories comprise one hundred dharmas that exhaustively encompass all phenomena; they are all manifested from the True Mind, just as images appear in a mirror without departing from it, such that no substantial entity can be found.
Question:

Regarding the first five unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), both their names and their substance are provisional; thus, they may be said to lack substantiality like shadows, similar to the aforementioned conditioned phenomena.

However, as for the unconditioned phenomenon of *tathatā* (suchness), its name is provisional but its substance is real, serving as the nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Why, then, do you say it lacks substantiality like a reflected image?
Answer: The *tathatā* (suchness) taught in this school is established only in contrast to the false; since it arises through such opposition, it remains itself a false dharma.
As the Sūtra below states: "To speak of the false in order to reveal the various truths—both the false and the true are equally dualistic delusions."
It is further stated: "The unconditioned has no arising or ceasing; it is unreal, like flowers in the sky.
The *Awakening of Faith* says: "From Perfect Enlightenment flow forth all pure True Suchness, Bodhi, Nirvana, and so forth."
"Thus, the dharmas of these five categories are manifested solely by the mind, all being identical to reflections.
Second, revealing the true and demonstrating the false to refute inverted sentiments, in two parts:
first, explaining the deluded sentiments by analyzing the dharmas, in five sections:"
I. Pointing Out: "Your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the wondrously luminous, true essence—the wondrous mind.
The mind manifests the body and mind just as a mirror manifests objects; yet the objects are not the mirror, for the substance of the objects is empty.
The mirror is not a [substantial] thing, for the substance of the mirror is real.
Since the distinction between the void and the real has been established, by this means the inversion [of perception] can be recognized therein.
Second, the refutation of the error.
"How is it that you have lost your original, wondrous, perfect, subtle, and luminous mind, and your precious, luminous, and subtle nature, instead recognizing delusion within awakening?

Mind is identical to nature; because its substance is all-pervading, it is "perfect" (*yuan*); because it is without obscuration, it is "luminous" (*ming*); because it possesses the dharmas worthy of veneration, it is called "precious" (*bao*); because it has been so from the very beginning and is not merely a product of the present, it is called "original" (*ben*).
The path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished; therefore, it is called "wondrous.
It is praised repeatedly, hence the words are repeated.
Awakening is precisely enlightenment, the nature of perfect luminosity.
Delusion is non-awakening; it is the delusory body and mind.
To awaken within the state of non-awakening is like a reflection appearing in a mirror, where the empty and the real can be distinguished.

Now, to discard the mirror-like fundamental nature and cling instead to the body and mind that resemble reflections—failing to distinguish between the empty and the real—is a great error. Therefore, it is said: "To recognize delusion within awakening."
What was previously called "names" is now precisely pointed out as the locus of perversion. Third, the description of delusion: "Obscuration becomes space;

within the darkness of space, the coagulation of obscurity becomes form. Form mingles with false thought, and the characteristics of thought become the body. Gathering conditions, it stirs within; rushing outward, it flees in pursuit."
Ignorance (avidyā) is dark in its essence, hence it is called "obscure darkness.
With ignorance within, the appearance of emptiness manifests externally; hence it is called "emptiness.
This constitutes the first turbidity of the kalpa (kalpa-kaṣāya).
The following text states: "From delusion and confusion, space arises. It further says:

"You perceive space pervading the worlds of the ten directions; space and seeing are not distinguished. Space exists but has no substance; seeing exists but has no awareness. These interweave through delusion to form this first layer, which is called the kalpa-turbidity (*kalpa-kaṣāya*)."
Within these three subtle states, the two phases of karmic transformation are also called "identity and difference" and "movement and stillness.
Because movement and stillness depend upon one another, within these two phases, form and color are formed in obscurity; this is precisely the root-body and the vessel-world.

Once form and color have manifested, perception dwells within them; as the perception of form and the object become intermingled, the locus of cognition constitutes the root-body (indriya-kāya), while the locus where perception becomes clarified and congealed is the receptacle-world (bhājana-loka). This is the third stage of manifestation.

Because there are objective conditions as objects, coarse consciousness is drawn forth; it discriminates moment by moment in an uninterrupted succession. Thus it is said: "Gathering conditions, it stirs within. These two preceding [states] are the coarse [aspects].

Because the continuity of mindfulness, through habitual perfuming, remains uninterrupted, it eventually becomes separated; as it grasps the characteristics of the six sense objects, its flow proceeds without ceasing. Thus it is said that it "rushes outward in flight"; this refers to the latter two coarse types of the *vibhaṅga-vijñāna* (separating consciousness).
From the subtle to the manifest, the three subtleties and four coarsenesses constitute the path of afflictions; here they come to an end.
Fourth, the manifestation of attachment:
"Taking this state of murky turbulence as the nature of the mind, one becomes deluded and takes this as the mind, becoming resolutely confused that it resides within the physical body."

People of the world do not realize that what is fundamentally ignorance has evolved into coarse agitation; they take this state of deluded confusion and turmoil to be the true nature of the mind. Once fallen into such deluded attachment, they remain resolutely unchanging, claiming, "My mind resides within this physical body. Consequently, they give rise to distinctions between sentient and insentient beings, and differences between those with nature and those without. To mistake this deluded mind for the Buddha-mind—how base is such a view!
5. Conclusion on Delusion:
"They do not know that from the physical body outward, including the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, all are things within the wondrously luminous true mind.
The sense organs and their seeds belong to the internal [subject], which perceives and grasps them as objects.

Mountains, rivers, and the great earth belong to the external; they are merely objects of perception (*ālambana*) and are not appropriated (*upātta*). These three types of objects are all the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Furthermore, this realm of space arises from delusive ignorance, for it is a transformation of consciousness;

the transforming consciousness itself is entirely ignorance, arising through delusion regarding the Truth, and likewise lacks intrinsic substance. Both the transforming consciousness and the transformed objects are images manifested by the mirror-like mind.
Therefore, the preceding text states: "Your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the True Mind.
Failing to understand this principle, you instead cling to the notion that your mind resides within the physical body; thus, this [passage] is provided as a concluding clarification.
2. Concluding the discussion by means of a metaphor to point out the characteristics of perversion:

"It is like discarding a clear, vast ocean hundreds of thousands of miles across, and instead recognizing only the substance of a single bubble, regarding it as the entire tide and exhausting the whole expanse of the sea."
The Tathāgatagarbha possesses four meanings, and is therefore likened to the ocean:

it is as profoundly deep as the ocean because it forever cuts off the hundred negations; it is as vast as the ocean because it encompasses the ten thousand dharmas; it is like the ocean’s precious treasures because there is no virtue it does not possess; and it is like the ocean manifesting reflections because there is no phenomenon that does not appear within it.
Its essence is profoundly still and quiescent, not corresponding with delusive defilement; therefore, it is called "clarified," which refers to the aforementioned meaning of profundity.
"Hundreds of thousands" refers to the aforementioned meaning of vastness.
Because they do not recognize this fundamentally pure essence, it is said that they "discard it.
They take only the state of deluded agitation as their mind-nature; therefore, it says, "they merely acknowledge," and so forth.
The entire tide, the great oceans, and the Bohai Sea are all different names for the sea.
"You all are people who are doubly lost within delusion; you are no different from my hanging down my hand."
"The Tathāgata calls such a person pitiable.
This concludes the preceding analogy of the finger.
To cast it into the great ocean is one delusion; to mistake the bubble for the ocean is a double delusion.
To take hanging down the hands as correct and holding them up as inverted is the first delusion.
To take holding the hands up as inverted and believing it to be correct is the double delusion.

First, an actual event was cited for verification; next, a metaphor was drawn for illustration; and in between, the principle was applied through progressive and regressive comparison to clearly point out the characteristics of correctness and inversion. How can you say that this is the "obliteration of characteristics"?
Let the wise examine this in detail.
Third, the true seeing is extensively and correctly revealed by means of the objects of perception.

In the preceding text, the non-arising of seeing was demonstrated by observing the river in relation to its opposite bank; however, that approach was superficial in form yet deep in meaning, remaining somewhat obscure and not yet fully explicit. Thus, it was not termed a "correct revelation," and the commentary describes it as a "coarse discussion gradually clarifying" the truth.

From this point forward, the text extensively addresses objects as conditions to dismantle names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), thereby revealing that this nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) does not fall into conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Subsequently, each section is harmonized and integrated so that one may know all phenomena (*dharma*) are illusory and fundamentally non-existent, and that there is only the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi. Because this is clearly and definitively established, it is said: "Correctly Revealing the True Seeing."
Section Four:
One, revealing that the perceiving mind is not an inherent nature, in two parts:
One, Ānanda recounts his realization and clarifies his doubts, in two parts: [1] Ānanda recounts his realization and clarifies his doubts; [2] ... (text continues)
I. Narrating the Realization.
Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction, wept and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Although I have received such wondrous sounds from the Buddha, I have realized that the wondrous, luminous mind is fundamentally perfect and complete, the eternally abiding ground of the heart.
"Because the Buddha extensively demonstrated the inversions to reveal the true mind, one awakens to the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*) that is signified by the vocal sounds that signify it.
Second, the manifestation of doubt."

“I have realized that the Buddha’s manifested voice of Dharma is perceived by means of the conditioned mind; though I have attained this mind, I do not yet dare to recognize it as my fundamental, original ground of mind.”
“I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim his perfect voice to uproot my doubts and lead me back to the Unsurpassed Way.
The Buddha uses words and sounds to explain this true nature, yet my current understanding and realization are still but the functioning of the conditioned mind.
The true nature you have realized and the conditioned mind by which you realize it are identical to what the Tathāgata previously reproached you for:
"As you now listen to my Dharma, this is a discrimination arising because of sound."
"What is the distinction?
Because of this, he did not yet dare to regard it as the "ground of the mind" (*cittabhūmi*).
The mind has the sense of being able to give rise to things and providing a basis for support; it is therefore metaphorically called "ground."

Regarding the term "perfect sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*): it refers to the fact that each and every utterance of the Buddha pervades the entire realm of sentient beings, yet its phonetic rhythms never become confused or disordered, as explained in the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*.
2. The Tathāgata’s explanation by means of analogies, in two parts:
first, identifying what it is not.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"You still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind; this Dharma is also a condition, not the realization of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Because of sound, there arises discrimination; this discriminative nature is itself subject to arising and ceasing."
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Do not use a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to expound the Dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
If expounding it is thus impossible, how could listening to it be possible?
One who relies on the conditioned mind merely relies on words and letters; therefore, it is said that such a person does not attain the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

If one can forget the self and merge with the Way, departing from the marks of subject and object, such that not a single thought arises and the boundaries of past and future are severed, this may be called truly attaining the Dharma-nature.
2. Revealing the fault through a simile, in two parts: A.
Refuting the recognition of the designator by means of clinging to the finger while losing sight of the moon, in two parts:
1. The simile, in two parts:
First, the dual delusion regarding the finger and the moon:
"Suppose a person points at the moon with their finger to show it to another; that person should look at the moon because of the finger.
If, however, they look at the finger and take it to be the substance of the moon, would this person not only lose sight of the lunar orb, but also lose sight of the finger?"
Why is this? It is because that which the pointing finger indicates is the bright moon.
The finger is a metaphor for the expressive verbal teachings; the moon is a metaphor for the truth expressed by those teachings.
If you wish to see the moon, you must set aside the finger to observe it.
If you wish to see your nature, you must set aside words to embody it.
If you cannot set aside words, how can you see your nature?
If one cannot even forget the pointing finger, how can one recognize the lunar disc?

The *Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith* (*Yuanjue jing*) states: "The teachings of the sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon; once one sees the moon, one realizes that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon itself. All the various verbal explanations and instructions given by the Tathāgatas to bodhisattvas are likewise so."
Both the finger and the moon are lost to them; both the expression and the meaning are forfeited, as can be seen from the text.
Second, both light and darkness are lost:
"Not only is the finger lost, but they also fail to recognize light and darkness."
Why is this? It is because one takes the substance of the finger itself as the nature of the moon’s radiance; thus, the two natures of light and darkness cannot be discerned.
Verbal teachings belong to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); because they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they are "dark."
Ultimate truth belongs to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because its nature is wholesome, it is luminous.
This can be understood through an analogy.
Second, the application (*yojana*).
"You are also like this. This is the application of the dharma to the analogy, as analyzed above.
First, regarding the guest's departure while the host remains, one censures the lingering conceptualization of conditions; this has two parts:
First, inferring the existence of a substance through the analogy of the Dharma:
three parts. First, the Dharma:
"If you take this discriminating voice of my preaching the Dharma to be your mind, then this mind should inherently possess the nature of discrimination even apart from the discriminating voice."

If one gives rise to a discriminating mind based on the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, this discriminating mind has no intrinsic nature from the outset; therefore, it belongs to the conditions of sensory objects.
It exists or ceases according to the presence or absence of those objects and is not permanent, being merely like a guest.
2. The Parable:
"Suppose there is a guest who stays overnight at an inn; having rested briefly, he departs and does not remain permanently.
Yet the person who manages the inn goes nowhere and is called the host of the inn."
This clarifies that the conditioned mind comes and goes according to objects, while the true mind remains serene and eternally present.
The "guest" is used as a metaphor for the deluded, and the "host" as a metaphor for the true.
Third, the synthesis.
"This is also like this: if it were truly your mind, then it would have nowhere to go.

As the following scripture says: "When sound is absent, there is no cessation; when sound is present, there is no arising. Being perfectly free from both arising and ceasing, this is the eternal reality."
2. Refuting the lack of intrinsic nature by examining objects of perception, in three parts:
first, establishing the lack of intrinsic nature by analogy:
"How can there be a non-conceptual nature apart from sound?"
In that case, how could it be that this mind which discriminates sounds merely discriminates my appearance, while being devoid of any nature of discrimination apart from all forms?
If this perceiving mind were the true nature, it should act like its master; how then could it come and go in accordance with the sounds?
Because there is no discrimination when sound ceases, how could it be the same as the true mind, which pervades the dharma-realm and remains eternally tranquil?
Just as it is with the mind that follows sound, so it is with the mind that follows form; therefore, it is said, "How could it be only... and so forth.
2. Pointing out the similarity to external schools:
"In this way, even up to the point where discrimination is entirely non-existent.
Previously, by citing form and sound, it was shown that the mind has no substantial essence; one should likewise proceed through all instances of fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.
Since this now transcends them, it is said that "even conceptual discrimination is entirely absent.
"Neither form nor emptiness" refers to those such as Kauśika, who obscure [this truth] by mistaking it for the *tattva* of darkness (*mṛtyu-tattva*).
It is not form because it cannot be seen; it is not emptiness because it arises through conditions and conjunctions.
Regarding what is called *mṛtatattva* (the principle of the obscure), it is sometimes termed *mṛtadhātu* (the obscure nature) or *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature).
In Sanskrit it is called *Sāṃkhyasāstra*, which here means "Number Theory" (*Sāṃkhya*); it establishes twenty-five principles (*tattvas*).
The first principle is called *prakṛti* (primordial nature), which they reckon to be eternal.
The twenty-fifth is called the *puruṣa* (spiritual self), which is also reckoned to be eternal.
When the self contemplates superior objects, *prakṛti* then transforms the twenty-three principles for the self’s enjoyment.
Since I experience [objects], I am bound by them as objects and cannot attain liberation;
if I do not think, the Primordial Essence (Prakṛti) remains unchanging, and since there is no longer any bondage, I am liberated—this is called Nirvana.
As stated elsewhere, "Kūśārī" does not refer to the Sāṃkhya school itself, but is merely a member of that class; it is mentioned here for the sake of illustration.
Third, the conclusion: a rebuke of the non-authority.
"When one is free from the conditions of all dharmas and abides in non-discriminative nature, then each of your mental faculties will have its own place of return;
how then can they be considered the master? The true mind is like the host, while deluded thoughts are like guests; guests come and go, but the host never moves."
If, apart from dharmas, you perceive a nature free from discrimination, this reveals that your mind-nature returns to each respective object; thus it would be a guest—how could it be called the host?
Second, demonstrating that the nature of seeing has no place to return, in two parts:
first, Ānanda follows the preceding discussion to raise a difficulty.
Ānanda said: "If my mind-nature has various things to which it returns, then how is it that the Tathāgata speaks of the wondrously bright, original mind as having nothing to return to?
I pray only that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me."

The term "nature of mind" (cittatā) applies to both the true and the false; what Ānanda clings to is the false, while what the Tathāgata points out is the true. Now, because he takes the arising and ceasing to which he clings and suspects it of being the wondrous clarity that has been pointed out, [the Buddha] says: "Then, how could the Tathāgata say that there is nothing from which to return?"
"Returning" (huan) is synonymous with "extinguishing" (mie).
Second, the Tathāgata distinguishes [the teachings] by way of contrast, in three parts:
first, he provisionally indicates and points toward [the truth] to grant permission for its exposition.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Furthermore, when you see me, that which sees is the fundamental source of clarity.
The word "furthermore" (qie) is a term of provisional expediency; it provisionally points to Ānanda’s mind capable of seeing as the fundamental source of clarity.
"Although this view is not the wondrous, subtle, and brilliant mind, it is like a second moon rather than a reflection of the moon.
You should listen attentively; I shall now show you the ground from which there is nothing to be returned."
This luminous origin is not the fundamental true nature; it is like the moon seen by one who presses upon their eye—it fundamentally does not exist.

That which is "not the moon's reflection" means it is not a reflection within water; rather, the moon’s reflection in the water descends from the true moon, which may be used as a metaphor for the wondrous response that accords with conditions and thereby achieves universal penetration.
What is perceived by pressing upon the eyes is entirely illusory, arising from diseased vision; this serves as a metaphor for how deluded seeing is fundamentally unobtainable.
It is precisely within this seeing that [the teaching] provisionally demonstrates its non-reversibility.
2. Clarifying through the objects to which [the faculties] may return;
this has two parts: 1. Clarifying that the objects have points of return;
this has two parts: 1. Listing the eight objects.

“Ānanda! This great lecture hall opens wide toward the east; when the sun rises in the sky, there is bright radiance. At midnight, during the dark fortnight, when clouds and mist shroud the heavens, it becomes dark and obscure again. Through the gaps of doors and windows, one perceives openness; within the walls and buildings, one observes obstruction. In places where distinctions are made, one perceives conditions; throughout the vast emptiness, there is everywhere the nature of space. When turbid vapors gather, they form a haze of dust; when the sky clears and the mists subside, one again perceives purity.”

These eight types of phenomena—light and darkness, penetration and obstruction, emptiness and existence, defilement and purity—are all established as their respective manifestations by relying upon causes and depending upon conditions.
2. Clarifying the Return of Each.
"Ānanda! You have all observed these various manifested forms; I shall now cause each to return to its original source."
What is the original cause?
Ānanda! These various transformations return their clarity to the solar disc.
Why is this? There is no day that is not bright; brightness depends upon the sun, and thus returns to the sun.

Darkness returns to the dark moon; passage returns to doors and windows; obstruction returns to walls and buildings; discrimination returns to its conditions; stubborn emptiness returns to the void; turbidity returns to dust; and clarity returns to a cloudless sky.
"Thus, all that exists within the world does not transcend these categories.
Since these eight objects both exist and cease to exist through conditions, coming and going, they are not identical to true seeing.
2. Showing that seeing has no place to return, in three parts: 1. The heading:
"As for these eight kinds of things you see, to whom would the luminous nature of seeing itself return?"
To be able to contemplate these eight kinds of views is called the luminous nature of seeing.
Since it is not produced by conditions, to what place should it return?
How could it be the same as the eight objects, each of which has its own destination?
2. Explanation: "Why is this?

If one returns to light, then at the time of non-light (darkness), darkness is no longer seen; although there are various distinctions such as light and darkness, the seeing itself has no distinction."
If true seeing is detached from conditions, yet those conditions still appear within seeing, then if it were to follow after the objects, who would perceive them later?
Objects naturally differ, yet seeing itself remains without distinction.
3. Conclusion:
"All things that can be returned are naturally not you; as for that which cannot be returned by you, if it is not you, who else could it be?
The eight objects can be returned, yet they are not your seeing. Your non-returning nature is precisely your true self. If this were not the truth, what else could be the truth?
3. Revealing delusion regarding reality to issue a reprimand:

"Thus you should know that your own mind is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure; yet you have become confused and distressed by yourself, losing your original nature and undergoing the cycle of rebirth, constantly drifting and drowning within birth and death. For this reason, the Tathāgata deems you pitiable."

"Previously, by presenting the eight objects to contrast them with deluded vision, I provisionally demonstrated that there is nothing that can be returned; from this, one knows that the fundamentally wondrous and luminous mind has never undergone birth or extinction. Yet, the originally existing true nature was lost in delusion and remained unknown, while instead clinging to conditioned objects and voluntarily undergoing the cycle of wandering."
As stated previously: "From beginningless time until this present life, because you have mistaken the thief for your son, you have lost your original constancy and thus undergo cyclic existence.
Although this was a provisional indication, its intent was to reveal that they are identical, because the derivative does not depart from the fundamental.
3. A further clarification based on essence and function, in two parts:
first, the posing of a question. Ānanda said:
"Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has no source from which it returns, how can I know that it is my true nature?

Ānanda’s intention in asking this was: previously, when the eight objects were confronted, the provisional pointing to the illusory seeing as having the quality of "returning" or "not returning" allowed him to recognize the fundamental, original nature as neither arising nor ceasing. Does this alone suffice to manifest the knowledge that the nature is eternal, or is there another distinct meaning by which one truly distinguishes between the real and the false?
Therefore, it is asked: "How is this known? and so forth.
Below, [the text] further explains that while there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority regarding function (*vṛtti*), there is no difference in essence (*svabhāva*).
Function is distinguished in relation to persons, whereas essence is discussed in relation to phenomena.
This, then, uses three preceding meanings to distinguish the True:
first, to manifest the absence of arising and ceasing; second, to clarify the presence of superior function; and third, to demonstrate the absence of differentiation.
Therefore, this response and explanation is divided into two sections:
First, a brief explanation based on the superiority or inferiority of their functions.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"I now ask you: at present, although you have not yet attained the untainted purity (*anāsrava-viśuddhi*), by relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power (*buddhānubhāva*), you see the first dhyāna without obstruction."
Having attained the realization of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one only then severs the delusions of discrimination; therefore, it is said that "the untainted [wisdom] has not yet been attained.
Lacking personal meditative power, one perceives by relying on another; therefore, it is said that "one relies upon the Buddha’s spiritual power."
The purpose of borrowing the power of penetration to allow others to see is that Ānanda intends to believe and know that the true function of his own seeing is such as this.
The foremost realms of the form realm—the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā—are all collectively termed the First Dhyāna.
"Furthermore, Anuruddha beholds Jambudvīpa as if looking at an *āmra* fruit in the palm of his hand.

Anuruddha is translated here as "Wish-Fulfilling" (*Yirui*) and also as "Free from Poverty" (*Wupin*). In the past, he offered food to a *pratyekabuddha*; for ninety-one *kalpas*, he has enjoyed wish-fulfilling bliss among devas and humans, lacking nothing whatsoever.
Before entering the Path, his nature was prone to excessive sleep; rebuked by the Buddha for this, he thereafter remained awake and consequently lost his sight.

The Buddha taught him to cultivate the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) in order to perceive worldly affairs; through this practice, he attained it and beheld the three thousandfold world system as clearly as looking at a fruit in the palm of his hand.
As clarified in the *Mahā-śāstra*, a great Arhat perceives a small chiliocosm; a great Pratyekabuddha perceives a hundred buddha-fields; and all Buddhas perceive all buddha-lands.

As for Aniruddha seeing the great trichiliocosm alone, it is because he has extensively cultivated the practice of mental attention (*manasikāra*); thus, among all śrāvakas, he is foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
As for the current mention of Jambudvīpa, since every great trichiliocosm contains a Jambudvīpa, there is no contradiction in using a specific term to manifest the general.
“Bodhisattvas perceive hundreds of thousands of realms.

Those on the first stage perceive a hundred Buddha-fields; those on the second stage perceive a thousand worlds; and so on, until those on the tenth stage perceive worlds as numerous as the atoms within immeasurable and ineffable Buddha-lands.
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions exhaustively perceive all pure lands as numerous as motes of dust; there is nothing they do not behold.
The Buddha possesses the five eyes and the three wisdoms, and that which he perceives extends to the very limits of the Dharma-realm.
The visions perceived by these four successive stages differ in their depth;
for the function of true vision unfolds according to what is realized through cultivation, becoming increasingly clear and far-reaching.
"The vision of sentient beings penetrates no more than a few inches.

Being separated by paper or film, one does not see external objects; being separated by skin, one does not see the internal organs. How can this compare to the function of true vision possessed by the sages of old?
Thus, the five successive layers of true vision and false vision can be clearly distinguished.
Yet you ask, "How do I know this is my true departure? Why do you not examine this for yourself?
2. A detailed analysis based on the fact that the essence [of seeing] is not a material object, in two parts:
1. The actual analysis that the essence of seeing is not a material object, in three parts:
1. Identifying the object.

“Ānanda! Let us first observe with you the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings dwell, surveying everything in between—those moving through water, on land, and through the air. Although there are various forms, both dark and bright, they are none other than the obstructions left behind by the discriminations of external objects.”
"Discrimination" (*vikalpa*) means differentiation; alternatively, it may refer to the objective realm that is discriminated, namely the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) which leave behind obstructions.
Second, the instruction for discernment:
"You should, in this regard, discriminate between self and other."
This is the exhortation.
You should, within this objective referent, attempt to distinguish between self and other to create a differentiation; "self" refers to the nature of seeing, while "other" refers to material forms.
"I shall now lead you to discern among these perceptions: which is my own substance, and which is the external object?
"Lead" (jiāng) means to request;
"which" (shuí) means what.
"I now request that you carefully examine and discern among what you have seen: what is the essence of your seeing, and what are those objects and images?
This is a direct exhortation to make a distinction.
3. The Correct Exposition, in two parts:
1. Clarifying that what is not a visual faculty is an external object (*viṣaya*). “Ānanda!

Exhaustively trace the source of your vision: from the palaces of the sun and moon, which are external objects and not you, extend your observation throughout the seven golden mountains; though there are various kinds of light, these too are objects and not you.

Gradually observe further: the rising clouds and flying birds, the moving winds and rising dust, the trees, mountains, and rivers, the grasses, shrubs, humans, and animals—all these are things that are not you.
"Ultimate" means exhaustive inquiry.
Investigate the nature of your seeing to its furthest extent: from the distant to the near, all that you see consists of material forms; these are not your own nature of seeing.
The mustard seed is a small herb.
Second, it clarifies that the perception of non-objects is the true nature. "Ānanda!..."

Although these various objects, whether near or far, differ in their inherent natures, they are all equally entrusted to your faculty of seeing, which is pure and clear; thus, while the categories of things possess their own distinctions, the nature of seeing is without difference. This subtle, wondrous, and luminous essence is truly your own nature of seeing.

"Though the categories of objects differ, the nature of seeing is always one; it does not vary according to the differences in objects, and this is precisely your true nature. This demonstrates that the true seeing is equal and without distinction."
Previously you asked:
"How can one know that this is my true nature?
Now it is clarified that while objects themselves are differentiated, the seeing-nature is without distinction; by this, one knows that this is your true nature.
II. Extensive Refutation of Mutually Dependent Attachments, in two parts: A.
Refutation of the Mutual Causality between Teacher and Disciple as the Basis for Perception, in three parts:
1. The Actual Refutation.
"If you see this object, then you must also be able to see my seeing.
If you insist on saying that you can see the mind and that it is distinct from the objects seen, [then you have not understood].
In this case, seeing would be identical to the object; the Buddha’s seeing of his own nature would likewise be an object, and thus it should be perceived by you.
Second, the refutation by way of reversal:
"If it were the same as seeing, then it could be called 'seeing me';"
"When I do not see, why do you not see the place where I do not see?
If you insist on saying:
"When I and the World-Honored One perceive the same object, since the World-Honored One’s seeing has already apprehended that object, my seeing of the object is precisely the seeing of the Buddha."
The scriptural passage is abbreviated, but it says, "He saw me.
This refers to what [the opponent] has calculated.
It is then refuted as follows:
"When I do not see, why do you not see the place where I do not see? This means:
when I do not take that object as a condition, it is called "not seeing"; you ought to be able to see this essence of non-seeing—why then do you not see it?
"If you see what is not seen, it naturally is not that characteristic of non-seeing.
This refutes a shifting argument.
If you persist in saying:
I also see the Buddha’s essence as non-seeing; what fault could there be in this?
Therefore it says, "If one sees non-seeing.
This is then refuted as follows:
